abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Heavy metal (HMs) contamination of soil and its adverse impacts are a global concern. However, limited studies have investigated the spatial and seasonal variability of soil HMs in the Tasik Chini area. This study aimed to assess the distribution, source, and contamination of ten particular heavy metalic elements (Cr, Cu, Co, Ni, Cd, Ba, Pb, Mn, As, and Zn) in the surface soil of the Chini Lake. A total of 60 soil samples were collected from 10 sites during wet and dry seasons, and analyzed using Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS). The degree of pollution was assessed using the CF and PLI, while PCA, CA, and correlation analysis provided insights into the prevalence and sources of HMs. Based on the findings, a notable mean concentration of HMs was measured in Ni (6.78 ± 8.37 ppm), Mn (11.51 ± 21.08 ppm), and Pb (3.23 ± 2.68 ppm), compared to background values of 16 μg/g, 460 μg/g, and 31 μg/g, respectively. Pollution indices revealed moderate contamination levels for Cd, Co, and Pb, especially in mining and agricultural areas. PCA indicates a variance of 50.27% with a strong relationship between As, Cu, Cd, Mn, Zn, Ba, and Pb, suggesting a common originating source of mining and agriculture activities. CA analysis highlights the higher contamination level in the mining area and downstream in the agricultural area among the sampling station groups. According to the results, human-made sources, including mining waste and agricultural chemicals, are the primary contributors of Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn, and As, whereas Ni, Cr, and Mn were mostly derived from natural geogenic backgrounds. This study concludes that seasonal inputs from mining and agriculture have a substantial impact on soil HMs contamination. Further studies are needed on ecological and socio-economic implications, including long-term monitoring, to support effective mitigation and management.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: HMs are metallic substances having a density of over 5 g/cm3 (Adnan et al., 2022a, 2022b; Ali & Khan, 2018; Chen et al., 2021; Feng & Wu, 2023). HMs describe a specific material class with metallic characteristics associated with ecotoxicity, pollution, or potential toxicity. These substances can be either metals or semimetals. Lead (Pb), asbestos, copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), iron (Fe), zinc (Zn), thallium (Tl), antimony (Sb), selenium (Se), molybdenum (Mo), cadmium (Cd), as well as several other compounds are among the metal(loids) that deteriorate the environment (Li et al., 2019a, 2019b; Vamerali et al., 2010). More than 20 million hectares (ha) of land are adversely impacted by HMs, including Cu, Cd, Cr, Pb, Ni, As, Hg, and Zn (Liu et al., 2018a, 2018b). The soil is an essential element of a terrestrial ecosystem and is fundamental for maintaining life on Earth. It is a reservoir for moisture and vital nutrients required for plant development. Nonetheless, because of its capacity to absorb and retain organic and inorganic pollutants, particularly hazardous HMs, there exists a risk that these contaminants may later be discharged into the atmosphere, aquatic environments, and biological entities (Wang et al., 2018; Wen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023a, 2023b). Some soils are naturally rich in HMs; however, certain anthropogenic activities can cause the HMs to be redistributed, which can pose environmental risks when concentrations are exceeded at certain levels (Järup, 2003; Marrugo-Negrete et al., 2017; Chowdhury et al., 2018; Rahman et al., 2019; Ali et al., 2019; Rajan & Janardhana Raju, 2023). An important agronomic practice that contributes significantly to the anthropogenic source of HMs is wastewater irrigation, fertilizer, and pesticides in the soil. Mining activities, including mineral processing, are additional sources of significant waste materials, including high levels of metals. These activities result in extensive mine tailings and large-scale sludge dams (Zhang et al., 2012; He et al., 2015; Clemens & Ma, 2016; Weldeslassieet et al., 2018; Hanf et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020; Kharazi et al., 2021; Bhat et al., 2022a, 2022b; Singh, 2024). The results from various studies carried out in Turkey, Bangladesh, England, Australia, and China indicate that the main human-induced factors contributing to heavy metal contamination in soils are primarily attributed to urban vehicular traffic (which includes emissions from vehicles, tire degradation, particles from worn road surfaces, and brake lining wear), industrial activities (such as power generation plants, fuel combustion, metallurgical processes, automotive repairs, and chemical manufacturing), the erosion of construction materials and pavement, as well as deposition from the atmosphere. Moreover, the key contributors of HMs that enter agricultural soils can be traced back to mining practices, processes of smelting, waste material disposal, runoff from effluents, handling of wastewater sludge, pesticide applications, and the usage of animal manures (Sezgin et al., 2004; Kojuncu et al., 2004; Ahmed et al., 2006; Alloway, 2013; Kachenko & Singh, 2006; Yu et al., 2008; Hajizadeh et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2019; Nawab et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2020; Rashid et al., 2023; Shakti et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Madhav et al., 2024; Rathod et al., 2024). These metals are highly mobile and xenobiotic (foreign to biological processes) and persist in the soil ecosystem (Huang et al., 2018). Mining activities and mineral processing generate enormous amounts of waste materials, including metals. Due to HMs' high toxicity, nonbiodegradability, and capacity to accumulate throughout the food chain, they pose a danger to human health, food security, and ecological processes (Li et al., 2023a, 2023b; Pandey et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2018, 2019; Zhao et al., 2020).

HMs contamination of the soil has become a global environmental issue in recent decades due to its persistent, toxic, and bioaccumulative nature (Priya et al., 2023; Edo et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2020; Rashid et al., 2023; Soleimani et al., 2024), especially in developing countries facing rapid urbanization and industrialization processes. This problem has garnered significant attention from researchers throughout the globe (Hou et al., 2025; Khan et al., 2024; Paya & Rodriguez, 2021; Qi et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2020).

Globally, numerous studies have assessed soil contamination, such as the pollution in Tabriz city, Iran: Cd, Pb, Cu, Cr, and Zn (Taghipour et al., 2013), in northern Colombia: Cu, Ni, Pb, Cd, Hg, and Zn (Marrugo-Negrete et al., 2017), and in various Chinese cities: pollution in Cr, Ni, Cu, Pb, Zn, As, Hg, and Cd (Wei & Yang, 2010; Zeng et al., 2019), Cd, As, Pb, Zn, Mn, Cu, Cr, and Hg in the Van area of Eastern Turkey (Yaylalı-Abanuz, 2011), Pollution levels of Pb, Zn, Cu, and Mn in Zwierzyniec, Poland (Mazurek et al., 2017); Cd, As, Pb, Zn, Mn, Cu, Cr, and Cd, Pb, Cu, and Co in Gebze, Kocaeli City, Turkey (Türkdoğan et al., 2003), Northwest region Guizhou, China Cd (Wang et al., 2022) above background limits. Prior investigations concerning HMs in precipitation from various nations, including Turkey, China, Iran, Mexico, the United States, Greece, Korea, and Tibet, revealed substantial metallic elements (Cherednichenko et al., 2021; Connan et al., 2013; Hosseinpoor et al., 2023).

Examining samples extracted from the Mynzhilki Mountains in Kazakhstan discovered marked amounts of lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd), copper (Cu), and arsenic (As) recorded at 1520, 206, 7720, and 275 µg/L, respectively. The northwestern area of France showed concentrations of Pb and Cd at 142 and 9 µg/L, respectively (Connan et al., 2013). Cukurluoglu et al. (2017) reported values for zinc (Zn), nickel (Ni), chromium (Cr), Pb, and Cd of 89, 4, 5, 10, and 13 µg/L, respectively, in Denizli. These metals are highly mobile and xenobiotic (foreign to biological processes) and persist in the soil ecosystem (Huang et al., 2018). These findings emphasize the worldwide significance about HM pollution and its transboundary traits.

Consequently, elucidating the intrinsic relationships and causal processes among soil characteristics and exposure to heavy metal threats is crucial for offering significant perspectives into recognizing and controlling soil HMs contamination (Jiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2024). Spatial analysis reveals the geographical distribution and clustering of HMs, aiding in the identification of prioritized control zones (Khosravi et al., 2018; Ran et al., 2021). Various methods, including PCA combined with multiple linear regressions, CA, and correlation analysis, have been used to evaluate the origins of heavy metallic elements (Chowdhury & Maiti, 2016; Hou et al., 2017; Islam et al., 2018a; Gabarron et al., 2018; Rasool & Xiao, 2019; Yuan et al., 2019; Fei et al., 2019b).

Tasik Chini is an inland riverine marsh recognized for its extensive animal and plant biodiversity (Khairil et al., 2011; Mushrifah et al., 2005). Due to the abundance of natural resources in the Chini watershed, UNESCO recognized it as a man and biosphere reserve in May 2008 (García Chevesich et al., 2017). The area around Tasik Chini has been developed for habitation, tourism, and agriculture, regardless of categorization (Marimuthu & Zakariah, 2020). In recent years, various studies have been conducted worldwide on heavy metal contamination, including source identification, distribution patterns, pollution levels, and threats to human health (Rastegari Mehr et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2019). According to our best insights, no research has been conducted on the spatial and seasonal change of heavy metal contamination in soil, especially mining and agricultural activities surrounding Chini Lake. There is still a significant gap in the complete assessment of soil pollution to seasonal variations. The present comprehensive study is the first to analyze the spatial distribution of HMs across different sites during the dry and wet seasons, and multi-statistical approaches have been employed to find the potential source of contamination. This research study addresses the present knowledge gap and provides critical insights for policymakers to better manage and preserve the Chini Lake ecosystem and its adjacent communities.

Therefore, the comprehensive study around Chini Lake is imperative for better resource management. The objective of this research study are to (i) To evaluate the spatial distribution of surface soil contamination level in the Tasik Chini Area, (ii) To investigate the contamination level of heavy metals in the study area using various indices, and (iii) To identify the heavy metallic elements contamination source using multivariate statistical techniques.

sec.title: Study area
sec.p: The second largest freshwater lake system in Peninsula Malaysia is Tasik Chini, or Lake Chini. It is located between (3.3750° N to 3.4667° N, 102.8778° E to 102.9695° E), consisting of twelve linked basins (Islam et al., 2015; Toriman et al., 2012). The lake is an inland surface marsh covering around 50 km2. It is a significant habitat for the nearby Orang Asli communities, both culturally and ecologically (Suhaimi-Othman et al., 2007). The area of the lake fluctuates between 150 and 350 ha based on season (Ahmad et al., 2008; Toriman et al., 2009). There is seasonal variation in the lake's depth, which ranges from 0.5 to 2.2 m. The range of the predicted volume is 4 to 7 × 106 m3 (Tan & Barzani Gasim, 2005); however, according to other researchers, during the dry season, the amount will drop by 606,000 m3 (Barzani Gasim et al., 2009). The tropical climate of the area is bimodal and humid, with an annual rainfall range of 1488 mm to 3071 mm and two distinct monsoon seasons. The most recorded rainfall was 3071.4 mm in 1994. The average annual temperature of the region is 21 °C to 32 °C and 2500 mm of rainfall (Harris et al., 2014; Sujaul et al., 2015). Every year, the northeast monsoon season starts from October/November until February. Since 1994, potential evapotranspiration has been estimated within a 500–1000 mm range. The Pahang River receives the lake's northwest flow, followed by the Chini River, which meanders for 4.8 km (Sujaul et al., 2015).

The Chini Lake basin originated from Permian felsic volcanics and volcano-sedimentary inheritances that feature volcanic-hosted significant sulphide (VHMS) deposits, which naturally saturate soils with Ni, Cr, Mn, and Zn (Basori et al., 2016). Furthermore, the watershed is impacted by decades of tin, iron, and gold mining (Rendana et al., 2023), as well as the use of pesticides and phosphatic fertilizers, which are significant carriers of Cd, As, and Pb. These inherent human-caused variables were taken into consideration when assessing the heavy metal sources in the current study.

sec.title: Soil sampling, preparation, and analytical analysis
sec.p: Metals enter the ecosystem via different sources and then accumulate over time (Abechi et al., 2010). Since contaminants are mostly concentrated in the upper 0–40 cm of soil (Krishna et al., 2007), suggesting that this surface layer is the most indicative of anthropogenic inputs and potential exposure hazards (Ogunmodede et al., 2015). Therefore, this study specifically investigated the pollution impact of anthropogenic activities on surface soil in the Tasik Chini.

Ten HMs were initially measured at a total of ten sampling stations throughout the lake during the wet and dry seasons: As, Cd, Co, Cu, Zn, Mn, Cr, Ni, Ba, and Pb. The ten sampling stations consisted of four in the agriculture area (AGS), three in the forest area (FAS), and three in the mining area (MAS), as shown in Fig. 1. The study analyzed the mean and standard deviation of these HMs in the soil.

sec.p: The samples were then sieved, and soil lumps were crushed. For every sampling site, three replicates of the samples were collected using an electronic vibrational core sampler tube (vibrator) to a depth of 0–20 cm (USGS, 2005). All samples were transferred to the lab for testing after being wrapped in polythene bags and cooled in an icebox. Each sample had a distinctive identification number based on location (Khan et al., 2018). To ensure a constant weight for heavy metal analysis upon their arrival, each sample was oven dried for the whole night at 105 °C (Han et al., 2016). The soil digestion procedure follows the US EPA Method 3050B (USEPA, 2010) regulations. 15 mL of concentrated HNO3, HF, and HClO4 were mixed with 0.5 g of soil using a Teflon breaker.

Following three hours of room temperature storage and wrapping, the samples were allowed to evaporate and eventually dissolve into a liquid solution. 5 mL of HClO4 was then added and evaporated to dryness. 10 mL of HCl was added to the sample and heated on hot plates until the mixture gained clarity. The solution was filtered and diluted to a 100 mL volume using deionized water in a volumetric flask. Finally, an inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometer (ICP-MS, Perkin Elmer, USA) was used to measure the HM concentration. A comprehensive QA/QC approach was applied throughout the laboratory analyses. The glassware and tubes were cleaned overnight with 10% nitric acid, rinsed with deionized water, and dried to reduce sample interference. Throughout the analytical quality control procedure, both blank and parallel samples were used. The accuracy and precision of the analytical processes were tested in triplicate using NIST reference material (Department of Commerce, USA). The recovery rate and accuracy of the operation were estimated to be 86% to 110% and less than 4%, respectively.

The standard method was used for measurement of soil Electrical conductivity (EC) and the value was obtained by conductivity meter (HACH 2100P). The soil organic matter content was determined using Weight Loss-on-Ignition methods at 500 °C. Soil particle size distribution was measured using Sieve and Pipette Method (Svensson et al., 2022). The soil texture classes were measured by plotting the percentage ratio of sand, silt and clay using the textural triangle (Soil Survey Manual, 2018). The selected heavy metals were analyzed using Inductively Coupled Plasma–Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) using the HF-HNO3-HClO4 in microwave digestion method (Parvez et al., 2023). In order to determine significant variations, the physicochemical soil quality parameters were evaluated using IBM SPSS software version 29 through Pearson regression and correlation analysis. The monitoring locations were arranged based on the level of contamination using the CA method. Potential sources of contamination were identified using PCA (Arafat et al., 2017). Cross-validation statistics were employed to analyze variations among the expected and noticed values after evaluating observed values against the interpolating values at a particular moment (Wilk et al., 2006).

sec.title: Spatial analysis
sec.p: Spatial analysis constitutes the systematic examination of the arrangement and interrelations of spatial data to identify patterns and trends. A variety of methodologies and frameworks are employed to scrutinize the spatial distribution, adjacency, and interactions of features or phenomena occurring on the Earth's surface. It usually utilizes Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to develop the spatial distribution maps carried out in this study. Ten heavy metal contaminants in soil for dry and wet seasons have been spatially distributed using the Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation methods (Mohammadi et al., 2023) in the catchment area around Chini Lake. The ArcGIS ArcMap software was used for analysis, mapping, and layout development. The elevation shown was extracted from the Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of the Shuttle Radar Topographic Mission (SRTM) version 3, having a spatial resolution of 30 m. The spatial variation of heavy metal concentration throughout the study area is shown by green to red colour codes (the values depicted in every layout legend.

sec.title: Physicochemical and Spatial variation of heavy metal content
Arsenic (As)
sec.p: The average concentration of arsenic (As) was 0.69 ± 0.58 ppm, ranging from 0.17 to 2.24 ppm (Fig. 2a). During the dry and wet seasons, station FAS7 recorded the highest arsenic content of 2.24 ppm, representing arsenic contamination localized hotspots (Kapwata et al., 2023; Nemati-Mansour et al., 2024), followed by the nearby station MAS8 (Fig. 2a). As concentrations of FAS7 raised during both the wet and dry seasons, indicating a continuous localized hotspot most likely connected to soil parent material and the use of land. The wet season showed slightly more variability, indicating hydrological impacts and surface runoff bringing agrochemical and mining ingredients (Aguilar et al., 2007), whereas the dry season indicated minimized transport and less mobility of As associated with the iron oxides (Bisone et al., 2016). The greatest As levels at FAS7 (forest) and MAS8 (mine) indicate influences from both natural lithogenic sources and mining-related elements, whilst the least level at FAS6 shows comparatively uncontaminated soils in forests. Arsenic naturally exists in ore-bearing strata (Fayiga, 2016; Gosar & Ajn, 2005); however, mining disruption can significantly increase its discharge and movement (Faria et al., 2023; Karczewska et al., 2013). As concentrations in soil and water vary significantly based on geological and environmental conditions. For example, arsenic levels in surface soils and during the pre-monsoon season ranged from 0.94 to 5.69 mg/kg in the Ambagarh Chowki block (Singhal, 2024). The least polluted station for arsenic during the wet season was found to be FAS6. A significant negative association was found between As and pH, EC, and sand (r = 0.630, P < 0.01; r = 0.594, P < 0.01; and r = 0.405, P < 0.01), respectively, indicating that a lower pH and a higher clay concentration may improve arsenic mobility and bioavailability. Conversely, As demonstrated a significant positive association with clay (r = 0.603, P < 0.01) and all selected HMs (Cr, Co, Mn, Cd, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni). This suggests arsenic may coexist with these metals due to related sources or geological properties (Kapwata et al., 2023). Both anthropogenic activities, like mining, industrial discharges, and the use of arsenical pesticides, as well as natural processes like rock weathering and volcanic activity, emit arsenic into the environment. Redox conditions, soil pH, and organic matter concentration are some of the variables that affect the mobility and bioavailability of arsenic in soils. These elements may impact arsenic's solubility and speciation, altering its environmental distribution (Zohra et al., 2024).

sec.title: Copper (Cu)
sec.p: The average Cu content was 0.92 ± 0.46 ppm, ranging from 0.14 to 1.83 ppm (Fig. 2b). Station MAS8 reported the highest Cu content, measuring 1.83 ppm during the dry season, while station MAS10 had the lowest concentration of Cu contamination during the wet season (Fig. 3).

sec.p: Cu concentrations increased at MAS8 during the dry period, probably as a result of increased adsorption and decreased dissolution in less acidic environments. Conversely, lower wet-season readings were a result of minimal mobilization and dilution processes caused by rainfall. Similar trends, where Cu contents are elevated during dry seasons due to decreased flow of water and sediment formation (Munksgaard & Lottermoser, 2010; Zhang & Xia, 2005), have been reported. As per Wuana et al. (2012) and Milazzo et al. (2014), rainfall under wet situations improves the leaching and movement of copper in soils and deposits. The greatest and lowest Cu levels were found at MAS, showing regional variation in pollution severity within mine-impacted soils. This fluctuation frequently results from variations in mining procedures, such as smelting and tailing destruction, which have unequal effects on Cu enrichment (Xia et al., 2023).

There was a significant negative association noticed among pH and Cu (r = 0.622, P < 0.01), EC (r = 0.0586, P < 0.01), and sand content (r = 0.0453, P < 0.01) in the Pearson correlation analysis. The inverse correlation with sand concentration (r = 0.0453, P < 0.01) indicates that soils with heavy sand content may exhibit reduced Cu retention capacity, resulting in lower Cu levels (Gharbia et al., 2022). Moreover, Cu is strongly associated with the selected heavy HMs (As, Cr, Co, Mn, Cd, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni). It implies that these metals may originate from similar sources or routes in the environment, including industrial activity or natural mineral resources (Manea et al., 2020; Niu et al., 2021).

sec.title: Cobalt (Co)
sec.p: Human activities and natural processes directly affect the concentration of Co in soils, like the production of Co Alloys and the burning of coal and oil (Gál et al., 2008). The average concentration of Co was 2.74 ± 1.89 ppm, with a range of 0.76 to 6.40 ppm (Fig. 2c). During the dry season, station AGS1 had the greatest concentration of Co at 6.40 ppm, while station FAS6 had the lowest pollution concentration at 0.76 ppm.

At AGS1, the Co amount exploded during the dry season, probably as a result of higher deposition in farming soils and less dilution from precipitation. On the other hand, reduced wet-season values indicate increased runoff-induced leaching and dispersion. Similar seasonal trends have been documented in other research, when low rainfall permits metal deposition in soils during dry times (Southwick et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2022). However, wet-season rainfall increases leaching and drainage, which dilutes and redistributes concentrations (Mimba et al., 2017). This suggests that AGS1 are more affected by pesticide inputs, whereas FAS6 are more consistent with natural baseline values. The application of pesticides and fertilizers on agricultural land might increase the buildup of HMs (Bucheli et al., 2023; Nuruzzaman et al., 2025), while indigenous biogeochemical patterns mostly govern forest soils (Baize & Oort, 2014).

Co exhibited a strong negative association with pH (r = 0.517, P < 0.01), EC (r = 0.374, P < 0.01), and sand content (r = 0.343, P < 0.01), indicating that higher concentrations of Co are associated with lower sand content, pH, and EC levels (Kosiorek & Wyszkowski, 2016). Moreover, there is a strong positive association with silt content (r = 0.364, P < 0.01), indicating that Co retains more in soils with higher silt content (Kosiorek & Wyszkowski, 2016); moreover, none selected heavy metallic elements (As, Ni, Ba, Pb, Zn, Mn, Cd, As, and Cr).

sec.title: Manganese (Mn)
sec.p: The manganese (Mn) levels varied from 0.43 to 99.22 ppm, with an average value of 11.51 ± 21.08 ppm (Fig. 2d). The highest Mn concentration was recorded at station AGS1 (99.22 ppm) during the wet season, while the least polluted station was MAS10 (0.43 ppm) for Mn during the wet season (Fig. 2d).

Mn concentrations increased during the rainy season, suggesting rainfall-driven flow and decreased pH, which facilitated leaching into lowland soils. Mn mobility is enhanced by acidic situations (Nawaz et al., 2013); however, land use and soil factors alter the level of bioavailability (Olia & Rezapour, 2021). The Sanjiang Plain has had similar land-use implications on Mn buildup (Zhang, 2011). This indicates that Mn inputs from fertilizer and pesticide use at AGS1 correlate with agrochemical enrichment in farming soils (Dhaliwal et al., 2023; Khoshru et al., 2023). On the other hand, MAS10 displayed lower Mn accumulation, probably as a result of geological limitations and restricted Mn movement in the deeper layers (Liu et al., 2018a, 2018b).

At station AGS1, the Mn concentrations peaked at 99.22 ppm, suggesting seasonal inflow. This is consistent with findings by Monjardin et al. (2022) and Sabijon et al. (2024), who identified enhanced Mn mobility in acidic and moist environments. Agrochemicals have a crucial influence on soil and water quality, particularly after rains, since studies have shown that their use contributes to higher levels of HMs, such as Mn (Imran et al., 2020; Neh et al., 2023). In addition, Mn leaching from chemically weathered soils into groundwater is enhanced by natural weathering during heavy rainfall, which exacerbates buildup in lowland soils (Gillispie et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2024). The findings showed a statistically notable negative association between Mn and sand content. Mn is less prevalent in sandy soils because they are generally more permeable and have a lower capacity to retain HMs (Sabijon et al., 2024). It shows that low saline sand carries higher Mn concentrations, probably due to the reduced movement of Mn in saline conditions (Monjardin et al., 2022; Sabijon et al., 2024); it suggests that Mn is more soluble and mobile in acidic soils, which is consistent with findings that Mn contamination is worse in low pH environments. A substantial positive association was observed among the chosen heavy metallic elements (As, Cu, Co, Cr, Cd, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni)this similar geochemical behavior is often linked to mining activities (Dube et al., 2024; Sabijon et al., 2024), and a moderately significant relationship was found with organic matter (OM) (r = 0.273, P < 0.05) represents Mn is retained more in organic-rich soils possibly due to the adsorption or complexation procedures (Sabijon et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2022a, 2022b). The mining area had the highest concentrations of Mn, followed by the agriculture area. The direct effect of mining operations, which discharge Mn into the environment, is shown in the maximum Mn concentrations in mining locations. Agricultural fields also show high Mn levels, probably because of herbicides and fertilizers, including trace metals (Dube et al., 2024; Sabijon et al., 2024). The Mn concentrations at different stations were consistent throughout the seasons, except for station AGS1. This might be due to increased runoff and leaching, which move Mn out of contaminated areas (Monjardin et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022a, 2022b). The concentration at station AGS1 showed a notable rise during the rainy season.

sec.title: Barium (Ba)
sec.p: Ba levels varied from 0.74 to 31.25 ppm, with an average of 4.26 ppm (Fig. 2e). During the dry season, AGS3 had the highest Ba concentration (31.25 ppm), probably because of the increased deposition and decreased dilution of airborne particles, which are more common during dry spells (Ebong et al., 2022), while FAS5 had the lowest (0.74 ppm) during the wet season (Fig. 2e).

The lowest wet-season levels at FAS5 represent rain-driven leaching and fragmentation, whereas Ba contents maximized in the dry period at AGS3, most probably as a result of atmospheric accumulation and confined dilution under limited precipitation. China and coastal basins have shown similar seasonal trends of Ba from atmospheric inputs and flushing caused by rainfall (Moody et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2014). Agrochemical use and potential mining-related inputs are likely accountable for the Ba enrichment in the soils of agriculture, as indicated by the highest level at AGS3 (Barillaro et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2022). In contrast, the low at FAS5 represents the baseline conditions in forest soils that are controlled by lithogenic processes (Watmough, 2014).

The content of HMs in soil is greatly affected by seasonal fluctuations. According to studies, the dry season tends to have greater concentrations of metals, especially Ba, because of decreased leaching and increased evaporation, which concentrates metals on the soil surface (Ebong et al., 2022; Osobamiro & Adewuyi, 2015). In addition, environmental elements like air deposition and local lithology are important. According to Tripathy et al. (2019), silicate minerals are a primary source of Ba in rainfall on the east coast of India, where regional lithology plays a key role. Ba exhibited a negative relationship with pH (r = 0.535, P < 0.01), demonstrating that barium concentrations often decrease with rising pH levels. This aligns with data indicating that Ba exhibits more excellent solubility and mobility under acidic environments, facilitating its release from minerals and soil constituents (Magaldi & Arfaioli, 2015), EC (r = 0.508, P < 0.01) implies that decreased Ba availability might result from increased ionic strength in the soil solution, perhaps as a result of competition with other cations for adsorption sites (Lamb et al., 2013), and sand (r = 0.354, P < 0.01) infers that Ba is more easily leached and mobilized in granular soils, which often have lower cation exchange capacity and organic matter content (Yoon et al., 2015), and sand (r = 0.354, P < 0.01) infers that Ba is more easily leached and mobilized in granular soils, which often have lower cation exchange capacity and organic matter content (Yoon et al., 2015), as well as an adequate association with Cr (r = 0.301, P < 0.05). There was a notable positive association found with clay (r = 0.381, P < 0.01), As (r = 0.769, P < 0.01), Mn (r = 0.828, P < 0.01), Cd (r = 0.830, P < 0.01), and Zn (r = 0.813, P < 0.01). The chemical structure of Ba influences its mobility and destiny in soils. The availability and mobility of Ba in the soil environment are impacted by its frequent presence in reducible forms such as BaSO4 and BaCO3 (Yoon et al., 2015). The soil's pH and organic matter level also influence Ba's distribution. According to Magaldi and Arfaioli (2015), alkaline circumstances may cause Ba to precipitate as insoluble compounds like barite, while acidic conditions might increase Ba release from minerals.

sec.title: Lead (Pb)
sec.p: Human activities such as industrial emissions, vehicle exhaust, and the use of leaded fuels are frequently associated with Pb pollution and have led to high Pb levels in urban and industrial regions (Arora et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2023). The Pb levels varied from 0.22 to 10.94 ppm, with an average value of 3.23 ± 2.68 ppm (Fig. 2f). The highest Pb concentration was recorded at station AGS1 (10.94 ppm) during the dry season. The least polluted station was MAS10 (0.22 ppm) for Pb during the wet season (Egorov & Prokofiev, 2023).

Pb concentrations maximized at AGS1 during the dry period, probably as a result of increased local inputs from agriculture and deposition and less leaching, whereas lower wet-season levels are a result of dilution and movement caused by rainfall. Industrial and mining locations have shown similar seasonal Pb patterns, with increased deposition during dry periods and discharge during the rainy season (Hossain et al., 2020; Mondol et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2024). According to Zhang et al., (2023a, 2023b) and Qin et al. (2022), Pb buildup is strongly connected with farming activities at AGS1, which is likely a result of pesticide and fertilizer inputs. Meanwhile, mining soils at MAS10 displayed comparatively lower Pb input, which is in line with the fact that Pb is frequently a secondary byproduct rather than the primary goal in these kinds of activities (Li et al., 2024). Pb revealed a negative association with pH (r = 0.424, P < 0.01), EC (r = 0.542, P < 0.01), and sand content (r = 0.486, P < 0.01). Ayu et al. (2024) suggest that these elements might affect their availability and movement in the environment (Silva et al., 2024). However, Pb strongly correlated with nine other HMs (As, Cr, Co, Cu, Mn, Cd, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni), indicating comparable causes (Gideon & Eyiseh, 2023; Widyastuti et al., 2024).

sec.title: Zinc (Zn)
sec.p: The Zn levels varied from 0.10 to 1.92 ppm, with an average value of 0.73 ± 0.50 ppm (Fig. 2g). The highest Zn concentration was observed at station FAS7 (1.92 ppm) during the dry season, followed by MAS8 (1.70 ppm). This trend is explained by the concentration of contaminants in water bodies due to increasing evaporation and decreased dilution (Dewey et al., 2023). The least polluted stations for Zn during the wet season were MAS10 (0.10 ppm) and FAS5 (0.26 ppm) (Fig. 2g).

The wet-season readings were lower because the rainfall stimulated dilution and runoff movement, whereas the dry-season Zn concentrations were maximum at FAS7 and MAS8, probably as a result of radiative concentration and decreased dilution. There have been reports of similar seasonal Zn fluctuations in semi-arid and estuarine situations, with dry-season buildup and wet-season flushing (Codling et al., 2020; Milazzo et al., 2014; Vizuete-Jaramillo et al., 2024). As a baseline with little human-caused disruption, the forest site (FAS7) probably represents natural lithogenic Zn inputs (Rutkowski et al., 2020). However, anthropogenic enrichment was found in mining sites (MAS8, MAS10), which is in line with research showing that smelting and ore processing operations raise Zn levels in catchments affected by mining (Karczewska et al., 2006; Palumbo-Roe et al., 2010).

The pH, electrical conductivity (EC), and sand all showed strong negative relationships with each other (r = 0.615, P < 0.01; r = 0.432, P < 0.01; and r = 0.451, P < 0.01), raising the possibility that low-conductivity and acidic environments might improve Zn availability and mobility (Maphanga et al., 2024). Conversely, Zn was associated positively with clay (r = 0.338, P < 0.01), highlighting that coarser materials such as sand are less efficient in adsorbing and retaining zinc than clay particles (Dewey et al., 2023) as well as with arsenic (AS) (r = 0.900, P < 0.01), chromium (Cr) (r = 0.582, P < 0.01), cobalt (Co) (r = 0.872, P < 0.01), copper (Cu) (r = 0.895, P < 0.01), manganese (Mn) (r = 0.872, P < 0.01), and cadmium (Cd) (r = 0.916, P < 0.01) suggest that these components could have similar environmental origins (Loto et al., 2023).

sec.title: Cadmium (Cd)
sec.p: The Cadmium (Cd) levels varied from 0.05 to 1.40 ppm, with an average value of 0.38 ± 0.29 ppm (Fig. 2h). Station MAS9 reported the lowest Cd content (0.05 ppm) during the dry season. In contrast, station MAS10 recorded the highest (1.40 ppm) during the rainy season, attributable to increasing runoff and human activities (Hellar-Kihampa & Mihale, 2023). (Fig. 2h).

During the rainy season, cadmium contents escalated, probably as a result of fertilizer leaching and improved solubility in acidic environments brought on by rainfall penetration. There have been reports of comparable rainfall-driven Cd mobilisation and leaching impacts in acidic agricultural soils (Ahmed et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2024; Hong-jun, 2008). The majority of cadmium pollution was linked to mining sites; however, the degree of contamination differed from station to station. Mining and smelting operations are commonly acknowledged as significant sources of Cd, especially in areas where Pb and Zn are mined (Luo et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2012). The same trends have been documented worldwide, with Cd hotspots frequently connected to mining operations near fragile ecological systems (Werner et al., 2024). Low cadmium concentrations are present in the aquatic environment as inorganic complexes such as carbonates, hydroxides, chlorides, or sulfates. Personal correlation analysis revealed a negative relationship between pH (r = 0.542, P < 0.01) and electrical conductivity (r = 0.450, P < 0.01), indicating that reduced pH and conductivity levels may augment Cd solubility and mobility in aqueous environments (Mosiienko et al., 2024), and sand content (r = 0.427, P < 0.01). However, it exhibited a strong positive association with silt content (r = 0.379, P < 0.01), revealing that organisms that live in sediments may be impacted by the buildup of Cd made possible by finer particles (Plaß et al., 2024) and all chosen heavy metallic elements (As, Cr, Co, Cu, Mn, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni).

sec.title: Chromium (Cr)
sec.p: The correlation revealed that Cr had a substantial negative relationship with PH (r = 0.633, P < 0.01), highlighting the increasing Cr concentration trends due to decreasing soil pH. The conversion of Cr(VI) to Cr(III), by acidic conditions, which is less mobile and hazardous, influences the Cr bioavailability and toxicity in soils (Cui et al., 2023; Zulfiqar et al., 2023) and a moderately negative association with EC (r = 0.263, P < 0.01) indicates the increased value of EC may diminish chromium mobility in the soils due to frequently linked with higher ionic strength (Cui et al., 2023), and sand (r = 0.291, P < 0.01). The Cr levels varied from 0.44 to 6.61 ppm, with an average value of 2.48 ± 1.18 ppm (Fig. 2i). In the dry season, station AGS4 had the highest concentration (0.61 ppm), whereas station AGS1 had the lowest value (0.11 ppm) during the rainy season.

Cr levels maximized during the dry period at AGS4, indicating lower dissolution and more retention under minimal precipitation, while the shortest rainy-season values at AGS1 indicate dilution and movement via runoff. Similar seasonal trends of decreased leaching during the dry period and increased mobility during the rainy season of Cr have been noted in polluted soils (Ahmed et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2024; Kessab et al., 2023; Mondol et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2024). The fact that both sites are on agricultural land indicates that, despite their varied circulation throughout farmlands, agrochemical activities contribute to Cr inputs. It is well known that pesticides and fertilizers, particularly those containing phosphorus and organophosphates, can increase Cr in soils (Moghaddas et al., 2013).

Seasonal variations in soil moisture and redox conditions may impact Cr speciation and movement. Moist conditions increase its degradation to Cr (III), while dry conditions may augment the stability of Cr (VI) (Xie et al., 2023). The association between Cr and pH is significantly negative (r = − 0.634, P < 0.01). A moderate negative association was found with electrical conductivity (EC) (r = − 0.263, P < 0.01) and sand content (r = − 0.291, P < 0.01). Conversely, Cr indicates a strong positive relationship with clay content (r = 0.640, P < 0.01) implies that more Cr might be absorbed by finer soil particles like clay, decreasing its mobility and bioavailability (Saleem et al., 2022) and with nine selected heavy metallic elements (As, Co, Cu, Mn, Cd, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni), this indicates that chromium contamination often coincides with other HMs, perhaps attributable to analogous sources or geological properties (Xie et al., 2023).

sec.title: Nickel (Ni)
sec.p: The average nickel (Ni) concentration was 6.78 ± 8.37 ppm, ranging from 0.05 ppm to 32.30 ppm (Fig. 2j). AGS3 had the highest concentration (0.32 ppm) during the wet period, followed by AGS4 (0.31 ppm). At station AGS3, the lowest value (0.10 ppm) was recorded (Fig. 2j).

Ni concentrations were greater during the wet season, owing to rainfall-induced leaching from mine tailings and worn primary material, but drier situations decreased mobility and reduced concentrations. Ni concentrations were much higher, which is consistent with findings that Ni often exceeds baseline values in soils impacted by mining (Zhang et al., 2023a, 2023b). Seasonal rainfall promotes sulfide mineral disintegration and Ni mobilisation in both water and soil systems, while acid rain enhances solubility (Godirilwe et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023a, 2023b; Wang et al., 2024). Conversely, decreased water circulation and hard pan development in tailings during the dry period restrict the movement of Ni and encourage the preservation of secondary minerals such as jarosite and goethite (Candeias et al., 2015; VanGulck, 2006). The impact of agrochemicals has been shown by Ni enrichment at agricultural sites (AGS3, AGS4). The pH of agricultural soils may be changed by fertilizers and additives to the soil, which also increase the solubility of Ni (Chuillier et al., 2004). In comparison, MAS stations had lower Ni levels, possibly due to decreased mobility caused by soil compaction and metal deposition.

The Pearson correlation analysis showed that Ni had a notable negative association with pH (r = 0.376, P < 0.01) indicate that the lower pH level could increase the solubility and dispersion of Ni within the soil environment (Luo et al., 2017), electrical conductivity (EC) (r = 0.520, P < 0.01) shows that the Ni availability could decrease by strong ionic strengths in the water (Luo et al., 2017), and sand content(r = 0.387, P < 0.01). However, Ni had an adequate positive relationship with organic matter (OM) (r = 0.290, P < 0.05), which shows that the association with organic compounds increases the retention of Ni in the soil (Luo et al., 2017), a notable positive association with clay content (r = 0.351, P < 0.01) denote the higher capability of Ni adsorbent may be due to clay-rich soil (Luo et al., 2017), in addition to with arsenic (AS) (r = 0.894, P < 0.01), chromium (Cr) (r = 0.480, P < 0.01), cobalt (Co) (r = 0.657, P < 0.01), copper (Cu) (r = 0.818, P < 0.01), manganese (Mn) (r = 0.742, P < 0.01), cadmium (Cd) (r = 0.791, P < 0.01), zinc (Zn) (r = 0.874, P < 0.01), barium (Ba) (r = 0.641, P < 0.01), and lead (Pb) (r = 0.868, P < 0.01) highlight the potential simultaneous contamination scenarios (Kumar et al., 2019). The environmental presence of Ni is impacted by both natural and human sources, including industrial emissions and waste disposal (Kumar et al., 2019).

Soil physicochemical characteristics, including pH, organic matter (OM), and clay content, are directly related to the dispersion of HMs. The present study discovered substantial negative associations between soil pH and metals, including Cu, Mn, and Cd, showing increased solubility and mobility under acidic circumstances, which supports the findings of Cui et al. (2023), Zulfiqar et al. (2023), and Mao et al. (2022). Metals such as Cu and Cd become much more soluble when pH drops; for example, at pH below 4, up to 90% of total Cd can be mobilized (Blake & Goulding, 2002). Metals are typically found in free ionic forms in acidic conditions, which are more mobile than their complexed counterparts at neutral pH (Shahid et al., 2025). Some soils have buffering capability that lessens this effect; however, Mn and Cd showed increased mobility around pH 5.5, especially in acid mine drainage zones (Tyler & Olsson, 2001; Zheng et al., 2024). However, favourable relationships with clay concentration and OM indicate that these elements promote metal retention by complexing and adsorbing metals. The development of metal–organic complexes is affected by both pH and OM content, whereas OM binds metals such as Pb and Cd, decreasing their mobility (Anjolaiya, 2015; Defo et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2018). According to Tan et al. (2018), clay minerals, including bentonite and kaolinite, improve retention because of their surface area and charge characteristics. According to Nenova et al. (2023), these interactions are further influenced by variables such as mineralogical composition and cation exchange capacity (CEC). Crucially, too much OM and clay can occasionally cause colloid formation, which may restrict the availability of sites of sorption (Anjolaiya, 2015). The concentrations of HMs may vary spatially due to variability in soil parent material and land use practices such as agriculture and manufacturing (Xiao et al., 2019), whereas vertical profiles indicate deeper layers of soil buildup of metals over time (Srinivasarao et al., 2014). These results highlight the intricate relationship that exists between metallic elements and soil chemical composition.

Overall, the distribution of HMs was significantly influenced by different types of land use. The highest concentrations of Ni, Mn, Pb, Co, and Cr were found at agricultural sites (AGS), mostly as a result of soil additives and the use of pesticides. The elevated amounts of Cu, Cd, Zn, and As found in mining sites were a result of mineral extraction and related leakage of waste. The lowest values were often found in forest soils, while lithogenic contributions are indicated by isolated hotspots such As and Zn at FAS7. These result indicates that mining and agricultural activities are the primary causes of heavy metal shifts in the Chini Lake watershed. These findings are similar to prior research by Shifaw (2018) and Rastegari Mehr et al. (2017), who found that fertilizer use and mining activities are the main causes of soil metal contamination in tropical conditions. The seasonal fluctuation of Cd, Pb, and Ni in agricultural and mining soils has significant consequences for public health, since wet seasons enhance the risk of transferring metals into foodstuffs and waterways. Studies from China's Guangxi and Henan provinces indicate that agricultural goods near mining areas were extensively polluted with Pb and Cd, frequently surpassing national food requirements and providing considerable health concerns to the local population (Liu et al., 2018a, 2018b; Zhang et al., 2020). According to Balabanova and Gulaboski (2015), such kinds of exposure are associated with chronic health problems such as neurological disorders, cardiovascular and kidney illnesses, and carcinogenicity. These results highlight the significance of land-use management strategies that control mining runoff and the usage of pesticides during periods of intense precipitation. Additionally, to guarantee food safety and lower long-term hazards to the public's wellness, consistent soil and crop assessment is crucial (Cheng et al., 2022; Shabalala et al., 2022).

sec.title: Contamination factor (CF) and pollution load index (PLI)
sec.p: Soil is classified into four categories depending on CF: < 1, low; 1–3, adequate; 3–6, significant; and < 6, extremely high. CF values for ten specified HMs during the rainy season are listed in Tables 5 and 6, and Fig. 4. During the rainy season, the range of Cd CF values was 0.05 to 2.45, but during the dry season, it was 0.20 to 2.86. The high CF value (2.86) was recorded at AGS2 and AGS3 at (1.91). The CF values were found under class II, which means moderate contamination and low. The CF values for other HMs were extremely low at the various stations, indicating low contamination. However, Co (0.10 to 0.53 and 0.06 to 0.29 during both dry and wet periods) and Pb (0.05 to 0.99 and 0.02 to 0.68 in dry and wet seasons) were significantly higher among HMs. However, they were categorized as underclass I (low contamination). Cd and Ni had higher CF values in agricultural and mining areas.

CF and PLI for the soil of 10 monitoring sites during the dry season

sec.p: Seasonal variations were noticeable, as CF values for Cd (up to 2.86 in the dry season) and Ni elevated under dry situations, indicating less dilution and more deposition in agricultural and mining soils. However, in several locations, CF levels decreased as a result of increased leaching and dispersion caused by wet-season precipitation. Similar trends have been noted, whereby a shortage of rainfall encourages the accumulation of metals, whilst a greater amount of precipitation encourages their dissolution and broader dispersion (Ebong et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024). All metals had a pollution Factor (CF) between low and moderate, although Cd and Pb had significantly higher values, especially at MAS9 and MAS10, suggesting localized pollution in mining and agricultural regions. This pattern correlates with findings by Al-Jbury and Al-Kasser (2023) in Iraqi urban soils, Yaylalı-Abanuz (2011) in Turkey, and Barzin et al. (2015) in Iran, where Pb was related to both natural and anthropogenic variables. Furthermore, Cd is well known to be a significant ecological risk factor in agricultural soils (Barzin et al., 2015; Dipti et al., 2023).

The mining zone recorded a lower PLI (0.072) compared to the rest of the lake area (0.24). However, according to the obtained PLI value, the lake soil is slightly polluted (Al-Jbury & Al-Kasser, 2023), indicating that the overall anthropogenic impact is still acceptable. The PLI results in this research were frequently lower than the threshold value of one, implying low overall pollution levels. Nonetheless, localized accumulation is suggested by higher PLI values at MAS9 and MAS10, which is in line with findings by Demková et al. (2017) and Dipti et al. (2023).

Despite the relatively low average PLI values, seasonal peaks at MAS9 and MAS10 indicate that significant precipitation events might temporarily boost the deposition of pollutants, which is in line with Demková et al. (2017). This represents the cumulative impact of pesticide inputs, discharge, and erosion during the rainfall season.

These findings are consistent with those of Waida et al. (2022) and Kowalska et al. (2018), who highlighted that cumulative environmental stress can be indicated by even mild PLI values in mixed land-use regions. The long-term persistence of HMs in soil despite cleanup attempts has resulted in higher PLI values in previous mining zones over time (Demková et al., 2017). Overall, these findings show localized but controllable contamination, emphasizing the importance of site-specific cleanup, particularly in Cd and Pb hotspots, as supported by Karimi et al. (2020).

Toxic metal deposition, such as Pb and Cd, poses major threats to the integrity of ecosystems, the quality of soil, agricultural yields, and human health, particularly in vulnerable communities in polluted regions. The findings of this study are consistent with recent studies by Widyastuti et al. (2024) and Yang et al. (2019), which emphasize the long-term ecological concerns presented by HMs in agricultural watersheds. The Orang Asli communities around Chini Lake, who depend entirely on the ecosystem for water, food, and cultural practices, are especially vulnerable, resonating concerns highlighted by García Chevesich et al. (2017) and Marimuthu and Zakariah (2020) regarding social-environmental stress in biosphere preserves. Pb and Cd contamination is mostly caused by air deposition from mining activities, and heavy metal buildup in soils and food crops is increased by polluted irrigation effluent (Hamoud et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2021). According to Bouida et al. (2022) and Mousavi et al. (2024), these metals can bioaccumulate in crops and aquatic species, enter the food chain, and cause long-term health impacts such as neurological diseases and renal failure. According to Luo et al. (2018), extended exposure to HMs also reduces soil fertility, endangering the sustainability of agricultural systems. These results highlight the critical necessity for continuous monitoring and efficient remediation in order to prevent ecological degradation and safeguard public health in rural areas that are at risk (Bouida et al., 2022; Mousavi et al., 2024).

The localized hotspots at MAS9 and MAS10 raised implications for persistent exposure to Cd and Pb, both of which are connected to potential hazards to neurological and developmental well-being, even though average CF and PLI values showed low to moderate contamination. Cd impairs mitochondrial function and promotes oxidative stress, apoptosis, and decreased neural communication by upsetting metal ion balance through Zn and Ca transporters (Arruebarrena et al., 2023; Wen & Wang, 2024). According to recent research, exposure to Cd changes cortical architecture and distinction between neurons in cerebral organoids, raising the possibility of long-term cognition and behavioral impairments (Dumpala et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023; Leal et al., 2012). Pb exposure is still a well-known risk factor for delayed growth and cognitive disorders in kids, with no acceptable blood lead level (Ettinger, 2022). Additionally, oxidative stress routes and increased amyloid-β and tau pathology have linked both Cd and Pb to Alzheimer's disease (Bakulski et al., 2020). The study emphasizes the significance of establishing cleanup plans tailored to individual locations and consistent tracking initiatives in mining and agricultural areas. To avoid cumulative effects on the safety of food and quality of groundwater, government officials should emphasize long-term soil quality evaluations.

sec.title: Source identification of metallic elements in soil
Multivariate statistical analyses
sec.p: The data obtained from experiments was evaluated by using a principal PCA and CA. The multivariate data were statistically analyzed using PCA. It aims to identify patterns within a dataset and reduce its complexity by transforming it into a smaller collection of new variables based on the correlation structure. The latest collection of a few variables includes the greatest data obtained from the source dataset, emphasizing its differences and similarities. Primary Component Analysis (PCA) is a reliable technique for lowering the Number of dimensions while keeping the majority of the information, since it is complicated to identify correlations in the enormous amount of data (Mukherjee & Singh, 2022; Smith, 2002; Wang et al., 2017). When the dataset contains more variables, it becomes more challenging to determine the variation statistically, as well as observe the variance and its relationship to covariance. In these situations, PCA is used to extract a more straightforward dataset. Through PCA, the collection of data associated with the p variable (Known as an analytical component) is transformed into a novel data set with p different multivariate components, known as primary components. A collection of data comprising linked or associated p variables (also known as analytical components). The linear function is known as the principal component of PCA. It combines the prior variables in such a manner that ensures their variance sums are equal to those of the primary variables (Olsen et al., 2012).

sec.title: Principal component analysis (PCA)
sec.p: Guan et al. (2021) used PCA on a large scale to identify metal contamination and sources in the soil. In the soil dataset, four main components with eigenvalues > 1 accounted for nearly 87.44% of the variation (see Table 7). The main part (PC1) with the most weight explained 55.27 per cent of the variation. It had strong relationships (> 0.75) with As (0.956), Cu (0.958), Mn (0.875), Cd (0.893), Zn (0.962), Ba (0.839), Pb (0.813), and Ni (0.880), but only moderate relationships (< 0.75) with clay (490). According to Hosseinpoor et al. (2023), this grouping is consistent with previous PCA research on multi-metal contamination in mixed land-use regions and indicates a major anthropogenic source, specifically mine effluents and agricultural inputs. The clustering of these metallic elements in PC1 further indicates their seasonal movement during the wet season, when rainfall-induced discharge and leaching boost co-transport into soils. However, the grouping of As, Cu, Cd, Mn, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni in PC1 (55.27% of the total variance) and the significant inter-metal relationships suggest a common human-caused source, particularly mine effluents and farming operations. This is aligned with the results of Singh et al. (2017) and Hosseinpoor et al. (2023), who utilized PCA to detect multimetal pollution clusters in similar land-use scenarios. According to Li et al. (2024), metals such as Cu, Zn, Cd, and Pb are higher in mining and smelting sites, accounting for up to 75% of overall pollution. The use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides has also been connected with rising content of As and Cd in agricultural soils (Wang, 2023), and higher concentrations of Cu and Cd in sediments adjacent to mining areas have frequently exceeded the norms for environmental quality (Levei et al., 2014; Moulatlet et al., 2023). It is difficult to determine the precise origin of As and Ni because natural geological processes also contribute to their existence, even though anthropogenic activities are the primary source (Bradl, 2005; Li et al., 2024). Similar investigations further validated these trends by finding that PC1 accounted for considerable contributions from urban wastewater in mixed-use watersheds (Karpuzcu et al., 2014) and substantial variation in contamination statistics, including 79.38% in an industrial zone affected by PCBs (Ilić et al., 2020).

caption.p: Rotated Component Matrix of HMs in the soil of the study area

sec.p: Therefore, metals like Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn, and As are mostly associated with human inputs from agriculture and mineral extraction, whereas Ni, Cr, and Mn partially represent natural geochemical backgrounds enhanced by sulphide deposits hosted by volcanoes.

We found significant positive correlations among these heavy metal elements, confirming their connections. PC3 explained 11.18% of the total variation in the pH variables, while PC2 explained 14.36% of the variation, with a heavy loading of silt (0.810) and a moderate loading of organic matter (OM) (0.498). We found that these parameters belonged to the same group, indicating significant positive correlations among soil properties (Hosseinpoor et al., 2023). In PC4, moderate loading on OM (0.651) accounted for 6.63% of the total variance.

The component plot (Fig. 5) provides evidence for this classification and grouping. Metals were also identified in acidic soil (pH = 4.3) in this study. Anthropogenic impacts, particularly mining, could cause a positive correlation among the HMs analyzed. According to García and Muñoz-Vera (2015), mining contaminates feeder channels in water reservoirs with HMs (mainly Pb, Cu, Mn, and Zn).

caption.p: PCA variance plot of physicochemical properties of soil in the study area

sec.p: The significant clustering of As, Cu, Cd, Mn, Zn, Ba, Pb, and Ni in PC1 suggests common origins, even though CF values were usually low to moderate across most locations, indicating minimal overall contamination. The concurrent presence of metals linked to mining (Cu, Pb, Zn) and agrochemicals (As, Cd) strongly suggests that human activities are the primary contributors, even though some of these trends may be a reflection of the basin's natural geochemical background (sulfide mineralization and felsic volcanics). Future research using normalized indices, such as the Enrichment Factor (EF), will be helpful in further distinguishing natural geological contributions from ones that are produced by humans.

sec.title: Cluster analysis (CA)
sec.p: HCA constitutes a statistical methodology that categorizes comparable entities into clusters according to their geographical resemblance and chemical composition (Maurya et al., 2019; Vega et al., 1998; Willett, 1987). Saraçli et al. (2013) have demonstrated that this approach is effective for grouping data items or similar variables. It groups comparable object data into a single group and finds similarities and differences between items inside a group. By increasing the degree of homogeneity or similarity, it is grouped into a single cluster. This study used Ward's approach (Fig. 6) to analyze hierarchical clusters to determine the best way to classify the station based on pollution. All indicators were considered in this analysis. Three clusters were identified in the surface soil analysis of ten sampling stations for HMs using HCA. The hierarchical cluster comprises stations AGS2, FAS10, AGS1, and MAS1, designed to have the highest loads. The second group includes FAS5, FAS6, and AGS4, categorized as moderately contaminated. The third group finally contained AGS3, FAS9, and FAS7, the stations with the lowest pollution levels. sec.p: The study's CA effectively separated mining and agriculture-dominated zones (AGS, MAS) from less affected regions (FAS) by grouping sample stations according to the degree of pollution. This is consistent with Wu and Su (2008) in groundwater systems and with Marrugo-Negrete et al. (2017), who noted comparable geographic clustering in lake basins. Despite the fact that PCA and CA are useful for locating sources of contamination and spatial patterns, it is crucial to recognize their limitations because not all contaminants will neatly fit into clusters that have been identified, requiring additional research into a variety of sources and transport pathways (Karpuzcu et al., 2014).

Additionally, this spatial grouping coincides with seasonal dynamics, as FAS soils exhibit less seasonal swings because of their inherent buffering capability, whereas AGS and MAS zones are more vulnerable to rainfall-driven runoff that carries metals from agricultural and mining operations. As a result, CA corroborated the PCA findings, demonstrating that land-use variations (mining/agriculture versus forest) are the main causes of HMs dispersion in the Chini Lake basin. However, it is vital to recognize that the basin's geology, notably its granite and volcano-sedimentary formations with sulphide mineralization, adds to the inherent baseline content of Ni, Cr, and Mn. The distinction is further reinforced by the geographical clustering, which shows that Ni, Cr, and Mn reflect a combination of geogenic and land-use impacts, whereas Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn, and As are concentrated adjacent to anthropogenic hotspots. To effectively distinguish between human and natural inputs in source allocation, future studies should include geochemical baseline values.

The integrated approach of PCA and CA confirms human activities from agriculture and mining while also providing a structure for prioritising controlling risk zones. These statistical techniques assist in directing healthcare initiatives by pinpointing areas that are at risk and need ongoing observation. In order to reduce the dangers of chronic exposure, environmental wellness strategies should include long-term monitoring of metal behavior, particularly under seasonal rainfall regimes.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study offers the first comprehensive examination of the seasonal and spatial variation of HMs in the soils adjacent to Chini Lake. It reveals that Ni, Cr, and Mn partially reflect natural geogenic contributions from sulphide mineralization, while Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn, and As are mainly associated with mining and agricultural operations. The significance of hydrology in improving dispersion and transmission into crops and water bodies is highlighted by increased wet-season values of Cd, Pb, and Ni, while dry-season stabilization promotes the buildup of Cu, Co, Cr, and Zn. CF and PLI results revealed low to moderate contamination, while isolated hotspots, especially at mining sites, raised concerns about long-term exposure. The lack of precise geochemical baselines and direct crops or water assessment prohibits robust identification of sources and risk estimation, regardless of the distinct contaminants trends found. Future study needs to address these deficiencies by including enrichment factors, ongoing surveillance, and food-chain analyses. The implementation of innovative remediation techniques, which include biochar amendment, phytoremediation, and microbial immobilization, as well as more stringent control of pesticide usage and better mine-waste management, is critically required for prevention solutions. Protecting soil quality, ecological stability, and the welfare of vulnerable groups, particularly the Orang Asli, requires continuous surveillance and policy-based solutions. The research findings draw attention to the importance of strengthening contamination management measures and enhanced environmental monitoring in this biosphere reserve to minimize ongoing hazards to soil health, ecological sustainability, and community well-being.
